utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. Mr. Mundis, is the Prosecution ready to continue the cross-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you then please escort Mr. Vorobev into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vorobev. May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony, and may I take it from you nodding that you hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'd ask that the witness be shown Defence Exhibit 185 and also that the witness be provided with a thin blue marker. And if the usher could place that portion of the map on the ELMO that shows the area marked by the witness yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, the area known as the Jewish cemetery is visible on that part of the map in front of you, is it not?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, if you could please take the thin blue marker and draw a line around the entire territory of the Jewish cemetery, please.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you drew a solid black line along the left-hand side, that is, on the western side of the Jewish cemetery; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you told --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you told us, witness, that the solid black line indicated the position of the Bosnian Serb army at the time you were posted in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also drew on the eastern side of the Jewish cemetery a dashed line, indicating the position of the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Along the northern side of the Jewish cemetery there is a transit road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I put to you that the ABiH forces -- that the confrontation line, if you will, the ABiH forces were along that transit road. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not always and not everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time you were in Sarajevo, from February 1994 onwards, were there periodic fire fights in the Jewish cemetery?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in light of the indications of the parties that you've drawn on that map, the Jewish cemetery in effect was no man's land; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Is there any need for re-examination, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should be happy, Mr. President. Could we put before the witness the original of the map.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the map can be, please, not rustled in front of the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That's okay, Mr. President. Thank you very much for your assistance in any case. [Interpretation] With your permission, Mr. President, in order to better see the map which is the same but it's the original in colour. And then on the copy which has certain changes. Yes. Can we show the witness the original. Mr. Usher, will you please take this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you going to tender the original or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just in order to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is merely to clarify certain things. And I'd like us to focus on the area of what is called Jewish cemetery, which is more clearly shown on this map, which is a colour map. And then I'll ask the same question of the witness, because there are different colours and it, therefore, allows us to distinguish things better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps before putting questions to the witness the original should be shown to the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask the witness to focus on this colour map and to scrutinise, to examine very carefully the area which is next to OP3 -- non-Cyrillic OP3, in other words the area of the Jewish cemetery. There. Yes, here we are. No. No. Thank you. That's it. Yes, the cemetery. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please place it as such that we also can see the observation post on the screen, a little bit up. Yes, like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Very good. This is perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, with the usher's help, we would like to also use the white-and-black map, which was used to also show the same area, but now we have the problem of markers, Mr. President. But don't put this map, please, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter says sorry, but they cannot interpret while the map is being rustled in front of microphones. We simply cannot hear speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, will you look at this blue line around the cemetery which you put it, and does it seem correct to you in relation to the original map? Can you look at both maps, compare them, and see whether you traced the outlines of the cemetery correctly.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously my eyesight is not the best because I think that I did not trace accurately the western side of the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Would you then agree with me, witness -- if you'd come closer to the microphone, please, for the interpreters -- would you then agree with me that the outline of the cemetery should be more to the east than the one -- than what you showed?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the west to the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, which marker should we use to indicate this correction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Green would be a perfect colour, if we have any green. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, witness, on the black-and-white map --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: -- Will you please re-draw the outlines of the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, witness. And my last question, which follows from the cross-examination: You were asked a moment ago about sporadic exchanges of fire around and in the Jewish cemetery. And my question is as follows: Did you ever, that is, you personally or your observers, did you ever see the fire being opened from the chapel -- from the synagogue or the chapel in the Jewish cemetery; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, personally I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And what about your observers? What about your observers?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: My subordinates reported through the duty officer that there were some armed men on the synagogue and that there was intermittent fire from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And when we talk about armed men, are we still talking about the army called the BH army?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the cemetery was on their side, I assume that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would seek leave to ask the witness a couple of additional questions in light of the corrections made to the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, the lines that you originally drew on the western side of the Jewish cemetery position the western boundary of the cemetery and the line held by the VRS as being virtually parallel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: To all intents and purposes, yes. But you will understand that the positions are never a straight line, that they always zigzag or something in order to better protect the personnel, the men on the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In light of the correction that you just made to D185 with the green marker, would it then follow that the line held by the VRS was along the line that you just marked with green?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, it was eight years ago since I left it, so of course -- perhaps I'm not a hundred per cent accurate when I draw it. I assume that this map when I gave it to Ms. Pilipovic, that it would help to discuss the subject, and now it seems that the map has become a stumbling block. I thought it would help us, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, again let me try to ask this as simply as I can: The line on the western side of the Jewish cemetery held by the VRS was approximately the boundary of the Jewish cemetery on the western side; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, witness, I'd like you to clarify two or three matters for me. Yesterday in your testimony you said that you had never heard - and I quote you - [In English] "I never heard the sound of heavy weapon fire from the Serb side." [Interpretation] What did you mean by "heavy weapon"? Would you say that mortars are heavy weapons, or are they not?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From 120 millimetres up. 120-millimetre mortars and other weapons of the same or larger calibres are to my mind heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So in this case, you can identify by the sound the calibre of a mortar?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, yes. But one needs to be quite near the position of the mortar because they are very loud. And when a shell flies, you can't hear it practically. You only hear it when it hits an object. Shots from tanks and guns sound louder, but it is very difficult to tell them apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. But to understand you correctly, you're saying that you never heard such mortar shots, or are you saying that you never heard shots from heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, never -- that means, when I was in Sarajevo. That is what you mean, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way. Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, right. Then I'll move on to another subject. You said also concerning the destruction of the city that, and I'm quoting, [In English] "There were some high-rise buildings that were destroyed in the early days of the conflict." [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, that would mean before you arrived in Sarajevo. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And my third and last clarification, please: You testified that you were present when General Galic issued orders to his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What were these orders connected to? Which subjects?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. They were occasional. Orders concerning the cooperation with me and establishment of posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it concerned cooperation with your unit.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the initial stage, immediately upon our arrival in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood you correctly, you were sometimes accompanied by General Soubirou, or rather, you accompanied General Soubirou.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So who took care of the translation? Were there interpreters that you had on your side or who were connected to -- or were interpreters connected to General Galic's command? Do you remember anything about this? Which language did General Soubirou communicate in when speaking to General Galic?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Soubirou had an interpreter who spoke Serbian as well. General Soubirou had his own interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But you didn't have interpreters from the United Nations who accompanied you. You didn't have your own interpreters from the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had four interpreters who spoke English and two who interpreted into Serbian. I had them in my battalion. They accompanied me to all meetings.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So these interpreters from the UN were present at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got a few questions for you as well, Mr. Vorobev. The first one concerns your answers in respect of traces on the asphalt of an impact you told us about. It was -- you told us that fragments were flying in a certain direction and that the shell would have come from the Muslim side, from the OP, observation post, 5 side. And you told us about the impact on the asphalt and that you could see something, you could draw conclusions as to the direction where that fire came from. Did you observe that yourself, or was it told to you?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw these traces myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the conclusions where the fire would have come from were drawn by yourself, or were you told what that traces would allow to conclude?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my battalion, I had a head of artillery who had spent his entire military service in the artillery and knew these things well. He knew what kind of shell leaves what kind of a crater and what the possible direction could be. He reported that to me, and I personally see a crater -- or rather, it was not a crater but a deep indentation in the asphalt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you check on whether his conclusions were right or not. I mean, were you able to check whether his conclusions would be the correct conclusions?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: When reporting to General Soubirou, I told him that we assumed that the shell had been fired from the observation post number 5, but we told him that it was our assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Assumption. But my question was a different one. My question was whether you personally, seeing the traces on the asphalt, whether you are able or competent to verify whether the conclusions that were given to you by your artillery specialist were correct or not.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you then, please, I have, on a blank piece of paper sketch or draw the pattern you saw on the asphalt and tell us why conclusions were correct. Perhaps it could be done on the ELMO so we can follow you.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crater had approximately this shape. If the fire originated from this side here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- yes. Could you please repeat what you just said. If the fire comes from this side. I couldn't see on the screen what you were pointing at. Yes.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the direction of fire was this one here, then the deeper part of the crater would be facing the source of fire. And I will, with your permission, draw the outlines of a shell. The head of the shell would make a deeper depression than the rest of the shell. So the indentation in the asphalt would be deeper in the area facing the source of fire, and it is produced by the head of the shell rather than the tail end of the shell. In addition to that, the majority of the fragments, shrapnels would be in front, in the frontal side of the crater, and some of them would be to the side. Fewer fragments could be found in the back of the crater. "In the back" meaning the one closer to the origin of fire. And this is approximately the scene that we could observe in the area where our battalion was deployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, you say that the density of the fragment traces would be higher in the back; that means in the direction of where the shell came from?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To the contrary of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the contrary. So the density would be higher in the front, so in the direction in which the shell landed and further onwards.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law of inertia provides that the majority of fragments would fly to the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Could perhaps that sketch be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or should that be -- as a matter of fact, it should not be marked for identification but it would be a Court exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it will be C3. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I just wanted to remark that the witness's response at line 13, 6 didn't appear in the transcript -- page 13, line 6. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness's response --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the witness responded in the affirmative. He said -- first his answer on page 13, line 2, it was, "No, to the contrary of that." I said, "To the contrary. So the density would be higher in the front, so in the direction in which the shell landed and further onwards." And I think then the witness confirmed that interpretation of his answer. Yes. Then another question for you, Mr. Vorobev -- Could perhaps the witness be shown again the large map. No, not necessarily -- it doesn't make any difference whether it's the original or the black-and-white copy. Could perhaps a part be shown -- oh, yes, it's in green. Could it be a bit wider if possible so that we have the area of responsibility. Even a bit more. Yes. Witness, Mr. Vorobev, when you were talking about the area of responsibility, I see that what appears in the original to be a green line which appears on the black-and-white copy, a rather dark line, in the north it's an uninterrupted line and in the south it's an interrupted line. Could you tell us what exactly does that difference stand for. So why in the north it is an uninterrupted line and why in the south it's an interrupted line. What does it indicate?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It simply means that there were two additional posts in the area of responsibility of the battalion that were not shown on this map, and these roads here, we used them to go to these posts. They controlled the positions outside of the exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you. I'm talking about the green lines. Are these roads or -- it seems -- what exactly do the green lines stand for, whether uninterrupted or interrupted?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It indicates the area of responsibility, the boundaries of the area of responsibility of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And why in the south it is interrupted and why in the north it is uninterrupted?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, in this area here we used this road in order to patrol, so that in order to show that the patrol went outside of the area of responsibility using this road, this is why we showed it in this way. In addition to that, there were several posts of the battalion which controlled the positions of artillery and anti-air defence of the Republika Srpska army, which was outside of the area of responsibility of our battalion. Some of the roads which are shown in these interrupted lines to the south of the area of responsibility of our battalion were used in order to reach those posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. And you pointed at where a red line crosses the green interrupted line. But if I go through the interruption of that line, to the right of what you just indicated, I do not see any road or -- I'm just trying to understand what that interruption you're just pointing at, what that means.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It basically doesn't mean anything special. There is no specific indication for the area of responsibility. My head of staff simply chose to indicate it in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My next question to you would be the following: Your answer to one of the questions of the counsel for the Prosecution when he asked you whether in effect the Jewish cemetery was no man's land, you responded in the affirmative. When a question was put to you about the chapel and firing from the chapel, you said that your observers or you - I'm not quite sure about that - assumed that the firing was from BiH military men since the cemetery was on their side.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the one hand side you tell us that the Jewish cemetery was no man's land, and on the other hand you say that the cemetery was on their side. Had this difference in answer to do anything with your position being, as far as I understand, in the rear of the Bosnian Serb line? Could you explain the difference.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say that the cemetery belonged or was controlled by the Bosnians. I said that the territory of the cemetery was neutral, or rather, a no man's land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The synagogue was in the immediate vicinity of the positions of the Bosnian army. And when I say "immediate vicinity," I mean 10 metres, within 10 metres. Since it was in the territory of the cemetery, they could have used it to open fire. When I -- to the question whether I saw armed men in the synagogue, I replied in the negative. I didn't see them. However, my subordinates which manned the observation post number 3 reported to me seeing armed men at the synagogue and reported also that there was intermittent fire opened from there. This is my final answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear to me. Did you ever receive any information about the involvement of foreign elements in the military forces around the Jewish cemetery? And with "foreign elements" I mean foreigners, so not citizens of the former Yugoslavia, participating in the units around the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We heard testimony both from non-former Yugoslavians, as from locals that were participating in these units about foreigners, and, as it was once called, weekenders, those who would come over the weekend to participate in units. You never heard about that, or do you have no personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. When you say that the BiH -- the presidency forces, that their positions were quite close to the chapel - you said 10 metres - have you any information as to if they would have been in the chapel how they would have entered the chapel -- through the door, through the windows, through the roof?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about a tunnel connecting the presidency forces with the chapel?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, Mr. Vorobev. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would seek leave to ask the witness a couple of additional questions concerning an answer he gave in response to a question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it is in relation to a question from the Bench, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you -- in response to a question from the Judge concerning the green lines indicated on the map before you, you told us "it simply means that there were two additional posts in the area of responsibility of the battalion that were not shown on this map and these roads here, we used them to go to these posts. They controlled the positions outside of the exclusion zone." With respect to the exclusion zone, how many additional posts did your battalion have that aren't indicated on this map?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two posts that are not indicated on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object. I object. I don't think that your Trial Chamber put any questions about the exclusion zone as such. There were questions about firing of heavy weapons, but there weren't any questions about the exclusion zone, so I don't think that this question arises from the questions put by your Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It arises from one of the answers the witness gave. And I asked him about the meaning of the interrupted and non-interrupted green lines, and Mr. Mundis is asking for a clarification of part of the answer. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, what was the role or responsibilities of your battalion with respect to monitoring the exclusion zones?

utterances.speaker: VICTOR VOROBEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: To ensure that the positions where the weaponry was held outside of the exclusion zone, within 20 kilometres of Sarajevo, remained the same. And should the positions be changed, we had to report to the commander of the sector in order for the measures to be taken concerning the removal of weaponry and in order for the weaponry to be placed in the established positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, when I allowed you to proceed, it was about the posts not indicated on the map you asked the witness about. Then the objection was that the exclusion zone as such was not -- had not been an issue, apart from just a reference -- just a short reference to it in relation to non-marked observation post. But I think that the Defence is right, that the exclusion zone as such and the implementation of that as such was not part of my questions. Neither was it a substantive part of the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Mr. Vorobev, this then concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you for coming a far distance to The Hague and to answer all questions, both of the parties and of the Bench, and I hope that you have a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Vorobev out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know if the next witness has already arrived, but you remember that yesterday the Prosecution told us that they would have one hour of cross-examinations. I hope the witness is here. We were -- we had a different schedule for -- a different time schedule. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We started at 9.00, not more than one hour. We are now three minutes to 10.00. But I do agree with you, that it went all a bit more quickly, which is, of course, highly appreciated by the Chamber, that we are using our time as efficiently as possible. The witness is there. But let me just confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the next witness is the only one on -- in whose respect we already gave a firm decision as to the protective measures to be granted, and that was facial distortion and pseudonym. What would be the pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DP35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: DP35. Then I'd just like to seek confirmation that the protective measures are in effect. They are not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you put in place whatever is needed for facial distortion. Yes. In the meantime, we could deal with the exhibits, since the public character is not affected by speaking about it. Madam Usher, could you -- Madam Registrar, could you please guide us through the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D185, map marked by witness; Exhibit C3, diagram drawn by witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no objection to those exhibits but would respectfully request that the colour map also be admitted into evidence in light of the fact that the witness referred to it and given that there are certain markings which are not necessarily visible or as visible on the black and white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would then suggest the following, if that would be agreeable to the Defence: That that portion of the map on which the Jewish cemetery appears, that that would be a kind of a subexhibit, because I think it's mainly the colour, that part of the map, that is of relevance for the issue. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. But the Prosecution would respectfully request we go a bit further to include the areas covered by the Russian Battalion, which would be the -- perhaps a couple of centre-pieces of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it then be agreeable that it would be -- I mean, if we put such a large map on a -- if we try to copy it once in one stroke, then that is rather costly. So therefore, would it be possible to have colour copies of the relevant parts put together? And if then, perhaps the Defence could show it first to the Prosecution, that the puzzle is -- that every piece of the jigsaw puzzle is in the right place, so that it could then be admitted as a -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what we suggest is to do a colour patchwork, to have a more admissible form, if I may say so, and to concentrate -- to take the more important parts of your map and to provide them to your Trial Chamber and to the Prosecution. But it seems impossible to us to copy everything for technical reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But parts could be copied and then put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. South south, east east, and west west. That would be a good solution. Then Mr. Usher, the -- first I have to give a decision on the admission into evidence. So D185 and C3 are admitted into evidence. And we -- Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So in order to avoid whatever confusion, D185 is the black-and-white copy of the map as a whole. The Defence is going to prepare a patchwork coloured copy of the relevant parts, and we'll see that and then admit it into evidence once the Prosecution has seen it. And C3, the diagram made by the witness, is also admitted into evidence. Then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort the next witness, DP35 into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, while waiting for the witness, could the Registrar please give me the next number so that I can put it in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, I will be taking this witness in cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, we are calling you this way because protective measures have been granted in respect of you. That means that your face will not be seen by the outside world, and we'll not use your own name but we'll call you Mr. DP35. Mr. DP35, before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And the text will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. DP35. Please be seated. I think the curtains can be raised again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphones for the witness please be adjusted, brought closer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please put the microphones a bit closer to the witness. Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. DP35, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I begin to examine Witness DP35, I'd like to produce a document to show it to the witness so that he can tell us if the information on the sheet of paper is accurate. Your Honour, I forgot to put the father's name on this piece of paper. It is my mistake. But if you wish me to, I will ask the witness what is his father's name or alternatively I can ask him to write it down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness did write it down already. Could it -- Mr. Usher, could you please give the copy to the ... Could it be shown to the Prosecution and to the Defence as well. May I take it, Mr. DP35, that the name you added on this piece of paper is the name of your father?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, I indicate that the witness added a -- with a green pen a name just where his own name is written down and not where it says "father" but that he now testified that this is the name of his father. Could you please verify the other parts of the document, Ms. Pilipovic, his name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, is the information on the sheet of paper shown to you accurate; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, can you tell us in so many words what education do you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: I completed the military academy, the AAD, and after that I attended a course for assistant commander for morale and political training and another course to become a chief of AAD, of the anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, can you confirm for us that between 1992 and 1994 you were in the territory of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you then in army service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was that with the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when did you begin to serve with the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and what post did you hold there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: From the 8th of July, 1992 -- no, sorry, 4th of July, 1992 to the 8th of February, 1993 I was the AAD regiment commander. And from the 8th of February, 1993 onward, chief of AAD in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that from the 8th of February, 1993 you were appointed the AAD chief in the corps command, can you tell us what duties does this office involve in a corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: The chief duties are laid down in the instructions which we used of the former Yugoslav army and which were then developed further in line with the conditions in wartime. And other duties would be the monitoring of the situation in AAD units of the corps, participation in the preparation of combat documents in the corps command to be used by AAD units, depending on individual aspects of the anti-aircraft defence, organisation and combat training of AAD troops, and air surveyance and reporting -- I could have also mentioned this in the beginning, because it is closely related to the anti-aircraft defence. In other words, the organisation of, training under the existing conditions in line with the then-rules, regulations, and instructions. Control, direct control of how the tasks are performed by the AAD units, extension of assistance on the ground, and requests are submitted to the corps command and the main staff to solve matters which could not be solved by units themselves or the corps was unable to solve. So these would be my chief duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, thank you. Before you listed to us the duties of the chief of AAD staff, you told us that you acted in line with the instructions and directives of the former JNA. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that you followed the rules of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes, we did. And I'm quite confident that other armed forces in the area did the same, because at that time they were -- it was impossible to draw up new rules and regulations, and these rules and regulations that existed were drawn up based on some conditions, terms, regulations outside the former Yugoslavia or outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, those developed by other countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us -- can you tell us if there is any difference between peacetime and wartime duties of AAD chiefs of staff.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No. The duties are identical. In peacetime, one carries out preparations within the AAD in case of need, because neither the army nor such units should exist at all if they prepared only for wartime.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, you told us that you were assigned to the post of the chief of staff of AAD from the post of regiment commander. Can you tell us, under whom was this regiment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: It was under the corps command directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you succeed somebody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: You mean the head of the AAD?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No, because it was vacant. And whilst I was a regiment commander, I discharged this duty in peril because I would go when and necessary to the corps command to do whatever was necessary to do in this relation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, who was the corps commander at the time when you were the chief of the AAD?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: It was General Galic [Realtime transcript read in error "General Mladic"].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As the AAD chief, did you become familiar with the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes. That was my duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think there is a mistake in the transcript. I shall repeat my question, but my question was: Who was the corps commander at the time when you received the duty of the AAD commander and you told me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Galic, but the transcript says a different thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before we interrupted your answer, will you please repeat to us if you became familiar with the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and counsel please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you not to start responding to a question when the letters on the screen are still moving, because the interpreters need some time to translate the words of Ms. Pilipovic, the new words. And this has already caused, I'm afraid, Ms. Pilipovic, that the words of the witness, at least, as I understood them, that when you repeated the question, that he then said "General Galic" and his words do not appear in the transcript. But it's not in dispute that the answer was "General Galic." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, before I resume my examination, I wanted to show the map C2 to the witness, since the witness has told us that he had become familiar with the area of responsibility of the corps. But we can show the map after the break. And I will move on with my questions without the map and then after the break we can put the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, can you tell us about the strength of the AAD and what about its equipment, how well was it equipped? In other words, how strong was your --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: We had 50 to 80 per cent of the materiel normally required, and the same would hold true of men. Specifically in the unit, in the regiment, it varied between 50 to 60 per cent of the full strength. And in AAD units, in brigades, that is, that was the same; whereas, the materiel standards varied, depending on the possibilities, supplies, and so on and so forth. If you want me to, I can add to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, wait. I'd like to ask you if you can tell us what about the level of training of the men.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: The level of the training under the conditions was quite satisfactory in terms of the tasks assigned to them, so that we can use a global mark and say that they were well trained.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the main task of AAD units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: The main task of the anti-aircraft defence units was to monitor the situation in the air space and general movement of a possible means of attack from possible air spaces, up to combat tasks. Secondly, support and defence of areas and zones where AAD units were deployed within the combat assignment of the corps as such. In other words, defence and fighting against fire points threatening our positions from the ground too, from land.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if in the course of your service you received some special assignments, you personally and your units.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Well, the assignments were not special. They were an integral part of the overall tasks of the corps command and had to do with assignments and regular duties of AAD units. And if there was -- if there was any emphasis laid on something special, it was for a unit to move, to relocate for technical reasons from one position to another, but this was mostly within the confines of areas and zones indicated in the initial combat assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, can you tell us, where were the anti-aircraft defence units deployed in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes. The units of the AAD regiment were deployed in the area of Lukavica, Donji Kotorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object to the question in its present form. It should indicate a time frame or a particular point in time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- it's my understanding that since the witness was asked about the time periods when he had responsibility in different functions, that he's mainly answering questions in view of his last position, that is, commanding the AAD in the corps. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 8th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think the answers of the witness should be understood in this way, unless there's any additional time aspect which we are overlooking, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my point is that that covers, I think, some 18 months. One assumes, given the nature of this weaponry, in particular its mobility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- That it cannot be assumed, I should say, that the positions remain throughout. That should be clarified first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps in one question -- perhaps we could ask the witness that if anything changed irrespective of any question put to you. So if anything changed after the 8th of February, 1993. So if your answer would not cover the whole period after the 8th of February, 1993, would you please indicate so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see you're nodding. But nodding does not appear in the transcript of this hearing. So I do understand that you agree that if on any question there's a need to make a distinction between a certain period after the 8th of February, you'll tell us. Yes? Mr. DP35, you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps having interrupted your line of questions anyhow, we could have a break now. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. And once he has taken his place, then raise the curtains again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, whilst the witness is being brought in, I note that a map has been placed in the vicinity of the witness box. Might I have the exhibit number of that map so that we can locate our copy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is C2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, before the break, you were asked about the positions where the AAD units were deployed within the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. If you know the position of these units in the time period from September 1992 to August 1994, to show them to us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: The positions of AAD units during that period of time did not change significantly. That means that the positions remained unchanged and only some weapons could have been moved temporarily and then returned back to their initial position. The positions of the units of the regiment of AAD was as follows: From Lapisnica to Pale to Trebevic, there was one battery with 20-millimetre weapons. Vrace, stadium Slavija at Lukavica --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, before you proceed to describing the positions to us --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order not to waste time, I would like the witness to point this out to us on the map, if possible, to indicate these positions of the units of the AAD regiment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, to your right you can see a map -- I'm sorry, to your left. If you can, please remain seated so that all of us can see the map.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you assist the witness such that his words can be heard by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, the mike is to your right, so could you please try to speak into it. And also, could you indicate east and west to us so that that can be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: The battery, as I've said --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's not possible for me to follow this evidence. In particular, the indications by the witness on the map. I'm not seeing it on the monitor, and given the angle of the map and the distance and the position of the witness in relation to the map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- I'm unable to follow it visually directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the Chamber will have similar difficulties, although the witness is not obstructing our view. It's at such a distance. Ms. Pilipovic, may I ask you. In how much detail do you want these positions? Are we talking about streets or about positions in general, that area, or ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we're not interested in the streets, just the positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So -- yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it then a practical way to do it -- I mean, we have -- we have other maps that can be put on the ELMO and that can be marked that we can see, so it's, of course, the level of precision you need and also the -- I don't know what areas the witness will bring us in, whether it's on other maps as well. But this is a rather impractical way of dealing with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence will put questions to the witness, and if we still have some time remaining at the end, then the witness can indicate then on the map the positions of AAD units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we still have some time remaining at the end of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Another -- so I think we have a couple of solutions to the problem: The first would be to use the same map but a copy of the map on the ELMO so that the witness points at that portion of the map on the ELMO, although the whole map is still there. And the other way would be to use a different -- a less-detailed map and ask the witness to mark on that map. But of course, I do not know where the witness will bring us. But please proceed. And perhaps during the next break we could solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, you started explaining to us where the positions of AAD units were from September 1992 to September 1994. So could you return to that question without indicating the location on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: I've already told you that the 20-millimetre battery was to the north-east from Lukavica command post. In the north-easterly direction, across Trebevic, Pale, and Lapisnica. 40-millimetre battery was in Vrace, stadium Slavija in the northern part of Lukavica towards Sarajevo. 30-millimetre battery was in Gornji Kotorac, Ilinjaca, towards the command post. 20-millimetre battery and 30-millimetre battery were in the Kaponiri airport. To the south, somewhat south-west of the command post in Lukavica. And finally, 30-millimetre battery to the south and somewhat south-east of Klanac. These were batteries which held firing position within the regiment. Brigade units were deployed in accordance with their areas of responsibility, which went from Lukavica through Mrkovici, Vogosca, Rajlovac, Ilidza, a part of Hadzici, Blazuj, Rakovica, and in Ilijas area, Cekrcici, Sevrle, Mrakovo. In the rear part some weapons were taken to Nisic Plateau where we had some units with AAD weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP35, if I understood you well, you spoke to us about the AAD units within the corps area and about the brigade units. Can you tell us whether all of these units were directly subordinated to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: The units were directly subordinated to me. The decision of the corps command was adopted in order for the regiment units to be used; whereas, the AAD units within the brigade were issued decisions by their respective commanders. Naturally I did have some influence regarding this, because I monitored the situation and I was familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP35, can you tell us, what were the tasks of the units which were directly subordinated to you, in view of your answer, from the 6th of September, 1992 up until the 10th of August, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: As I have told you in one of my previous answers, the main tasks were to monitor the situation in the air and to prepare for anti-air defence or anti-air combat. But based on the tasks that units had pursuant to instructions, the units which were in direct contact with the corps command also had tasks that had to do with direct support to the units in whose area they were in order to provide air defence from the ground and fire at various spots in the air that were deemed to be a threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, before we turn to targets and -- did I understand you well that you received your tasks from the command of Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: I received from the corps commander, but while -- I also participated in the preparation of the orders and instructions. I gave proposals, and the commander would decide on each of my proposals. He would either adopt it or modify it. That's an answer to the first part of your question. And now the second part of your question had to do with targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, I want to clarify something regarding your previous answer. When you said that you received your orders from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps command, from the commander, can you also tell us how did you receive them. Was it directly from the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps or was it from the chief of staff of that corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: I was in direct contact with the chief of staff, but I could also receive some of my tasks directly from the commander, because we worked as a team within our staff, and the commander whenever possible followed the preparation of every combat document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the preparation of a combat document," can you tell us whether you received your orders in written or in verbal form before the document was prepared.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Based on the written document of the superior command, the commander or chief of staff would inform about the combat situation and about the task facing us. So basically he would read it out. And based on that all of us within our all-respective fields would assess the situation and give proposals for the final decision, order, and combat order.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you as chief of AAD were always in the command or were you executing tasks in the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Some of my tasks had to be discharged within the command, but the majority of my tasks had to be discharged in the field due to the fact that the units were quite dispersed within the area of responsibility of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the AAD units of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps were active within the time period between September 1992-August 1994, and if so, in what way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: The units were active in this period of time. I would like to point out that they were active in defending the positions because they were deployed within their respective brigades. That means that they opened fire against targets which threatened our combat positions using all weapons available to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "using all weapons available to them," can you tell us what weapons were at the disposal of the AAD units and how were these weapons used.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: When I talked about the deployment of batteries - and I mentioned their calibres - I told you that the first weapon at their use was a 20-millimetre three-barreled gun, and we used targets which were 1500 metres away. These were visible targets. We didn't use all three barrels due to our technical capabilities. We only used the middle barrel and would use short bursts of fire or individual shots. The second weapon was a 30-millimetre gun with the range of 2.000 metres. We used two barrels also to fire against direct targets. A 40-millimetre one-barrel gun was used also against firing targets, up till 3.000 metres. There could also be light armoured vehicles which normally have a thinner metal as their armour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP35, based on your answers so far, it seems that the AAD units in the relevant period of time were not used for anti-air defence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, because there were no air raids at the time. We also had a battery called Aero 2M [phoen], which could reach targets up until 2.000 metres in the air. However, it was not used during that period of time because there were no air raids then.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP35, I would like to go back now to the issue of targets. You spoke about your targets. Can you tell us, did you have targets? And if so, what constituted a target for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: For us targets were fire points, meaning positions of different kinds of weaponry, excluding armoured ones. And I'm referring to the enemy weapons here, the ones that we could damage or destroy within the ranges that I've already described to you. So this mostly had to do with fire points, with combat or non-combat vehicles that could be discerned in movement and for which we could assume that they either transported deadly weapons or explosive material.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, did you as chief of AAD have some kind of a map? How did you register, if at all, these targets or fire points, as you call Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 17490 to 17496. them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No. We didn't use the map for targets and fire points except in the zone of separation that you can see on this map, providing that we knew the exact positions. However, those positions which were of any use to us were quite distant, and we mostly targeted those targets which when active came close to the separation line. So the ones that approached our range.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, for the sake of the transcript, the witness was pointing at the map C2, and he was pointing to the western part of that map where the confrontation lines goes first north and then north-east, that area. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, during the time we are interested in, did you personally keep records of the targets in the course of your unit's activity? And if you did, in which area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Well, throughout the entire area mostly, but mostly where the regiment was. This is the south-eastern part. A minute ago I indicated the entire zone, and the south-eastern part where the majority of the targets were. These targets weren't recorded in any special manner but through additional documents, such as notebooks, they were recorded and registered. And the fact that the targets were there -- or rather, firing points, was something that was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, when you say that you kept these notebooks, these working notebooks, did you personally have such a notebook for an area where you had marked the targets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No. Notes were made in the notebooks with other information and details, and each chief had a plan for the use of his units. To be more specific, in addition -- I had a map like this map, and it was entitled "An anti-aircraft defence plan, corps command." And the boundaries had been -- the boundaries of the corps and the brigades had been marked on the map, and the position of the anti-aircraft units. So as chief, I wasn't that much interested in the position, in the deployment. I was less interested in the position of the enemy's land forces. But if I did have information about air targets, about the directions of advance, then something would be marked on the map in an empty part with a plan of possible targets and where aircraft might come from. In the cases when we had combat with firing points and points on land, we didn't make such markings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So I have understood you to say that the firing points on the land, on the ground, were not marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally have some sort of an aide memoire, something that would help you remember these things? Did you mark the targets in the area from which enemy forces were active?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Not for targets on the ground, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, apart from the duties of an AAD chief, which was the main task you had in the corps, did you have to perform any other duties? Did you have another post from September 1992 up until August 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to performing the duties of the AAD chief, the staff organs also carried out other tasks in the team, in the leading team, in the leadership team of the command, and this had to do with solving certain issues in the area of responsibility of the corps, especially when the commander was absent from the command post or the chief of staff. And this leadership team worked in the operation centre where operations were carried out. I spent more time there than in my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that you would spend more time in the operations centre, can you tell us whether you had a certain task or certain duties and can you tell us where this operations centre was located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: The operations centre was part of the command. It was within the command. It was in the vicinity of the other premises, and the command consisted of ground floor and the one floor. It was directly linked to the most important offices. It was linked via telephone, and we carried out tasks in that operations hall in which we had working maps and other documents, and that is where we would receive reports and where we would inform the commander if he was in the command or somewhere out in the field, regardless of where he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, I don't think you have fully answered my question. You told us that you worked in the operations centre. My question was whether you had a certain position there or whether the people who worked in such a centre had a certain position, certain titles, in order to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes. There was an officer of the leading team. This was one of the commander's assistants. They would change -- these assistants would change. And the chiefs of service branches and officers from the command organs were members of the leadership team and of the operations -- an operations duty officer. So mostly it was the role of the operations duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So as far as I can understand you, you had -- you played the role of the operations duty officer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, who designates the operations duty officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: The chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Given that you had such a role, can you tell us what the tasks of the operations duty officer were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Well, the tasks of the operations duty officer consisted of monitoring the situation in the corps' zone of responsibility. That means in the command and in all units. Secondly, the daily -- the regular daily reports, which would arrive in written form, in encoded form, they would receive these regular reports and if necessary, irregular reports, extraordinary reports, which would be communicated via telephone in encoded form depending on combat situation and the particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just confirm whether I have understood you correctly. You spent quite a lot of time in that operations centre. From the time when you arrived in the corps, February 1993, up until August 1994, how much time did you spend in the operation centre? How frequently were you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: I would be there for at least an hour every day. It depended on the task and on whether this was necessary. When I was on duty, it would be up to 20 hours. When there was intense combat activity, I, as part of the leadership team, would be there, and how long I would be there depended on how long the combat activity lasted. It could be something between two and twenty-four hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP35, while you were performing these duties, while you held this position, did you receive written or verbal protest from UNPROFOR or from the BH army? And if so, who forwarded them to you and how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: We did receive protests in the command from -- not directly from the BH army. They didn't arrive in the operations centre directly from the BH army. They were sent through the liaison officer, the liaison officer for UNPROFOR. We were made aware of each protest because it was our duty to report to the commander about this, to inform the commander about this, and we would follow how this protest was developing on the basis of the commander's decision and the task that he assigned. The task would be to check to see whether such an incident had occurred, the incident with regard to which a protest had been lodged.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, could you please be more specific and tell us when you would receive such protests, whether it was from UNPROFOR or from the BH army, through the liaison officer, can you tell us something about the contents of these protests. Do you remember anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: I can remember some of the protests. I can't remember all of them, of course. But in each protest which was lodged and in which victims were mentioned, this would be checked in the field. We tried to determine whether it was possible for one of our units to open fire in the field. I could provide you with some examples too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. DP35, you say that the protests mentioned casualties. Can you tell us whether the names of the casualties were mentioned in those protests, the location under which circumstances -- did these protests contain detailed information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No. Just the area was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So when you would receive such a protest in which the area was mentioned, if I have understood you correctly you would check to see whether the units in that area had been active. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes, you have. I would suggest this to the commander. A team would be formed if necessary in order to check this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, you have told us that you can remember some examples. Can you tell us whether you personally participated or acted on a protest.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes. As operations duty officer, at the beginning of February 1994 I received via the media, via the radio, information according to which our units had been active and their action had resulted in casualties in the Dobrinja region. A team was formed. The chief of staff formed a team. And the team tried to establish whether there had been such action. This wasn't confirmed. And the liaison officer for UNPROFOR never provided an official protest, either written or some other form, but we were only informed about this via the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, you have told us about checking the information obtained through the media. After such information had been checked, as you say, did you make a written record of this check-up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes. And in the daily operations report, this would be forwarded to the main staff of the army. They would be provided with a report. The chief of staff or commander would be provided with this report. And such report would be sent to the main staff with this person's signature and authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP35, while you were an operations duty officer, did you ever receive a protest from UNPROFOR and did you check such protests?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: With UNPROFOR members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So when you say "yes," does that mean that you personally went to check up on this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this occurred and do you remember which area was concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you. I can't give you the precise date, but towards the end of January 1994 -- and yet again this information came through the media first of all. It stated that our units in Ilinjaca and Gornji Kotorac had fired on a tower for guiding aircraft at the Butmir airport. The liaison officer informed the commander about this. He informed General Galic about the event. Since this concerned a position where one of my batteries were located and UNPROFOR members appeared with Captain Leon Kolp [phoen] as their head - I think that was his name - I was given the task by the commander to visit that position as the chief and to establish which positions could have been used to fire at the tower at the airport. We did this for two days, and we established that it was not possible to hit the tower with the weapons that we had at our disposal.
