At the same time on the Igman side - that's the Muslim side - there was another team working there, and the leader of the team, Captain Leon, told us that our situation was quite clear, and he said that the airport tower had been hit from above Hrasnica, from part of Igman. I don't know how it was hit. Not much damage was caused, but it wasn't possible to cause this damage with my artillery. When we returned from the field, I informed the commander -- or rather, the commander was absent at the time, but we informed the liaison officer about the details, because reports would be forwarded through him. And in my presence, Captain Leon thanked us and he said that he wanted to thank General Galic and myself, as someone who had participated in this control, he wanted to thank us for behaving professionally and in a very correct manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. DP35. I understand the fact that you needed to be a little more expansive in your response, but what I am interested in is whether there was some sort of written record which was made when you and UNPROFOR members went to the site of these incidents.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: I didn't make any kind of record. Members of UNPROFOR made records, and the liaison officer made records, but I had no access to it after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP35, while you were chief of the AAD - and you told us that you were also the operation duty officer - did you personally attend meetings of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes. On a daily basis when I was in the corps command if I wasn't in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who attended those meetings and whether General Galic was also present at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes. General Galic would chair the meetings if he was there, if he wasn't in the field. And if he was absent, the chief of staff would chair the meetings, or the first official from among the assistants. So in addition to the commander, the assistants participated, members of the leadership team and of service branch organs from the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague will now continue with the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good day. I would like to continue with this line of questions that concerns the meetings in what we call the operations hall. But before we turn to this matter, I would like ask you the following question: Do you know whether there was a sniper unit - and I am saying "sniper unit" - within the army corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No. Such a unit did not exist as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would now like to go back to the subject of protests, and more particularly to the subject of protests for alleged shelling in the rear of the demarcation lines themselves. I think that you had the occasion to see such protests; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes, I did have the occasion to see such protests in the operations centre. I have provided some examples in which I participated. I participated in solving them in a certain way, but there were certain protests -- and I didn't participate in solving them but I was familiar with them. One example was then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I apologise. I'll interrupt you. I'm talking about the rear of the lines. And when I use this term, I am referring to the part of the city of Sarajevo which remained under the control of the BH army. I'm not referring to the lines themselves, not to Butmir or elsewhere. Did you see such protests?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. According to what you know as operations officer and as someone who was in charge of the AAD units, was it possible that the elements that we were talking about were justified by the presence of military targets - that is to say, of legitimate military targets - in the area of shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: I can't provide you with a more detailed answer because the means that the anti-aircraft units had at their disposal weren't such that they could fire at such targets. All I could do was help with the explanations of some of my associates who have such means. And I'm referring to artillery primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether in the part of the town that we are talking about now, do you know whether there was a certain number of military objectives concealed in that part of the town, legitimate military objectives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes. I know that there was a certain number of objectives, targets, command posts, ammunition warehouses, the exit from the tunnel which had been made from Sarajevo to Butmir and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like us to go on discussing this question about shelling and protests, and I will therefore ask you the following: Do you know or can you tell us how many men under arms were in the part of the city that we are talking about, that is, in the other army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. I object to the question. It contains no reference to either year, month, day, or even time of day, and no reference to sources. There's no restriction in the question to sources of information that the witness might rely upon in giving his answer. And finally, the question of my learned colleague has not sufficiently defined the area of Sarajevo, to use his words, that we are talking about. That's unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, since I take it that the witness has not counted them personally, could you please be more specific in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I could do that, Mr. President. But as regards the part -- the part of Sarajevo that I was talking about, I don't see why things are not sufficiently clear to the Prosecution, because on the one side, we have Serb forces, and on the other, Muslim forces. But I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, my attention was just drawn to the fact that the witness has answered the question in such a way by saying that he did not. So I -- if he doesn't know, I take it that it's in the largest sense you'd like to put your question to him. Please proceed to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if there was a major difference between the number of troops available on one side, on the side of the BH army, and the other side, that is, the army that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: I did not have accurate precise information, but from other members of the command and the staff I could hear that the ratio was almost drastic and that it was somewhere between 1 to 2, that is, 1 to 3. In other words, that in Sarajevo there were three times more men under arms in Sarajevo than around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Now I'd like you to focus on my question. When one is in such a situation where one of the forces outnumbers evidently the forces of the other side, of the other army, can one then say that it is a legitimate strategy to seek to reduce this imbalance, that is, to seek to eliminate as many forces as possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. The question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I say this with the greatest of respect, is nonsensical. This was war. Whether or not there was an imbalance in the number of troops, imbalance in the sense that one side had more than the other, more troops, does not legitimise to a greater or lesser degree the armed conflict. This sort of question does not assist the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, quite the reverse. Quite the reverse. Because if in a city the ratio is 1 to 3, according to this witness, then the question is whether those who are smaller in number will try to do something to change this ratio, which is highly unfavourable to them, and this can tell us very many things, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first try to find out what the facts were. Mr. DP35, may I ask you, was it the strategy of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to eliminate as many persons serving in the opposite army, that is, the army that was in control in the city itself, the often -- often called the presidency forces or the BiH forces? Was that the strategy of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the question whether this would have been a justified strategy or legitimate strategy is not relevant any more. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what type of weaponry did your adversary force defend against you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: I did not go into the core of their defence. This was something that was done by my associates. I was aware that they had no air force, but we had misgivings about that. We had to expect it. We had to anticipate the use of the NATO air force and we were proven correct, even though this is after the period of time that we are talking about. But apart from the general knowledge, I know that they had infantry weaponry practically of the same types that we had, also they had at their disposal regarding the gear of my type, perhaps a smaller number of pieces than I did. I know also that they had armoured vehicles and artillery pieces, but I cannot give you the numbers relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm now moving on to another question. In terms of distance, that is, in terms of the technical possibility, your batteries or some of your batteries, were they in a position to fire and hit the part of the city that I was just talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Are you saying that your batteries were too far to be able to aim it and hit that part of the city? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Besides, they could not fire at the urban part. They could target at the Butmir part and the area towards Sokolovici, which was open and which was not inhabited, because my pieces cannot fire at -- or rather, cannot destroy buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were there -- witness, were there in the army which is yours certain AAD pieces which -- of considerable calibre which were not under your control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: They were -- all AAD pieces were under control. They were direct control and indirect, because they were in brigades. Indirectly through brigade commanders or chiefs of AAD in brigades and commanders of the batteries there. There were no independent AAD units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And therefore, witness, am I then to deduce logically from this that since your weapons could not -- were outside the reach of the city, or rather the other way, because your weapons -- because the city was beyond the range of your city [as interpreted], then they did not fire during the period that we are talking about. I'm talking about your AAD pieces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: They did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. I object to leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if during the period under consideration any order was ever issued by your officers or you to use those weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No. There were no such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I'd like us now to address your contacts with General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You said that you spent a lot of time in the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the last question. I wonder if there are some words missing. Perhaps I should raise it at this stage rather than later. "Witness, do you know if during the period under consideration any order was ever issued by your officers or you to use those weapons?" Was that further qualified in relation to civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that about AAD pieces or?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question -- the question should be as follows -- yes, indeed, in order to shell the town, that is, how I worded it. And indeed this is lacking. The target which is the city and the fact that we're talking about AAD weaponry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... In order to avoid whether confusion, once rephrase your question as you intended to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you've already answered, but perhaps it is a matter of the transcript, and therefore I will put the question to you in different words. Did you - you personally or your officers - ever issue orders to fire from your weaponry on the part of the city which had remained under the control of the army called the BH army? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I move on to another series of questions, witness. You told us that you spent a great deal of time in what you call the operations room, and there, therefore, you could meet, I presume very often General Galic or frequently. You could see him there frequently. Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel and witness please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know if General Galic spent more time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's a request that you make a pause between the answer and the next question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us if General Galic spent more time in the headquarters, that is, in Lukavica, or in the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: All in all, about the same. At times he spent more time in the corps command, and at times he would be more often, because we had our forward command posts, and he also spent quite a lot of time there. And besides, we also maintained direct communication with those forward posts. So it is difficult for me to say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. And when a protest would be lodged with you by whomever, concerning, for instance, a case of shelling, and you would then transmit this report to your superiors, this protest which then reached General Galic, what did he do with it? Did he do it professionally? Did he do it carefully? Did he do it how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Well, I do not think that he simply glanced over any such protest. The check would be made, depending on the type of the protest. It would be checked through the relevant brigade, relevant unit, or a team would then be sent, which would be assigned by the corps command, and it would involve experts, that is, qualified persons, persons qualified for the types of weaponry allegedly used. And that again went through liaison officers, which means that UNPROFOR received feedback on such an activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But professionally and humanely, how would you qualify General Galic, since you knew him personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Well, in my view, as for his humane qualities or his professional qualities, well, of course it is not mine to judge my superior. I can only give some personal view. I always respected my commander professionally and from the point of view of command, and while we worked together in this command, I never heard any order that could be considered inhumane. A war is a war is a war. And there are combat actions, and that is different from what you call humanitarian contexts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, since you are telling us about this aspect of things, since you were close to your commander, I'd like you to focus on a question: Did you personally ever hear any mention by anyone in this command circle in Lukavica about a plan at the corps command the purpose of which would be the eradication of the Muslim population from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No. Quite the reverse. There was no such plan, but all our activities were aimed at preserving the Serb population around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, does that mean that you were undertaking principally defence actions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher now please help us to show some documents. I believe we have the following numbers. Just a moment. Excuse me. I have to check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the help of the usher, please, with the Chamber's leave, we should like to offer certain documents, 1491, 1492, 1493, and 1494. Mr. President, perhaps we could proceed logically by producing the first of these documents, which is the one which ends in "91," that is, 91. I will, therefore, show them in sequence to the witness. Every document is in Serbian and is accompanied by its English translation. I will repeat: We should produce them in chronological order, ascending order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you used now eight lines to indicate that you would follow the number -- the numeric order. If you would have done so, we would have had no difficulties in following you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, will you please be so kind as to read this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: I understand this document. I participated in its preparation. I participated in its processing. And I think it is quite clear that we complied with the existing standards and that we accepted these movements of the humanitarian aid by air, and this was also, as you can see, sent to the SFOR command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Will you please now move on to the next document, again, chronologically speaking, and will you read that one as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could have it, Mr. President, on the ELMO so that everybody could read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Have you been able to read this document, document 1492?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And the same type of question for item 3 that we see in this document; in other words, are you familiar with this kind of document and have you seen it, when, and so on and so forth, and what can you tell us about its contents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Since it has to do with the humanitarian relief, we were quite clear regarding the situation, and I think that the real conditions were we complied with such documents and such orders, and we never prevented nor did we allow to prevent the delivery and distribution of humanitarian relief or passage of humanitarian relief through our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, will you please focus on item 3. Item 3 refers basically to the protection of certain persons in wartime conditions in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. And first I'd like to ask you: Are you familiar with this document? Did you see it at the time? And so on and so forth. What do you have to say about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't be able to comment on item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. But my question is: Such instructions to comply with the conventions as such, were they issued relatively frequently at this particular level?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: I cannot say that they were issued relatively frequently. Such instructions were issued whenever the need arose or if something -- or if some change had occurred in relation -- in comparison with the previous situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'd like you now to move on to the next document, that is, the document 1493. Will you please read it, and pay special attention to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: -- To look at the date and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We could not hear which paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you talk into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm sorry. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind as to look at the date of this document, please, and then the three first passages, the first three paragraphs of the text.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes. I've had a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you confirm for us the reality that is reflected in this document? Can you confirm the date? And as for the contents of the document itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. And it was done as ordered, as we can see, that is, who it is delivered to. And it was delivered to the units, as we can see, because this was a unit that had to do with me. It was light AAD. It also received this document, which means that all the units received it and we were able to check whether the lower-ranking units were also informed about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just to clear things up, I'd like the witness to read point 2-1, which we have in the Serb document, "to ensure the reception" and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Will you read it, witness, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: "To ensure the reception and visit control and unfettered and safe movement of UNPROFOR teams and humanitarian relief convoys across the territory of Republika Srpska along authorised routes and at the authorised time." I don't think that anything is unclear here. The units that were related to me did not control either checkpoints or roads or anything. And their job was merely not to allow that such convoys be targeted, but it never happened from our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. And now I'd like us to concentrate on the last of the documents, and that document is 1494. Will you please look at that. Can you read this document, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes. I am familiar with this document, because it falls directly under my jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, each one of these documents which were shown you, that is, four documents that you were able to see, could you please confirm for us the authenticity of the signatures, that is, in those documents which you identified. Can you tell us, were they indeed signed by the person whose name is indicated there every time at the bottom of every document? Were these documents signed by that person at that time? And, therefore, meaning that that person then issued those orders at the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes. The documents were received by the AAD regiment here on the document, and the name of the commander -- we do not see the signature. Why isn't there a signature? Because we can see that on the left-hand side there is a signature of the person who issued the order. When it is on the left-hand side, it means that the message is coded and sent as such. And when you receive it coded -- and it cannot be coded if the document is not -- has not been signed. So this was coded, and it is so guaranteed, since the regiment received it and verified it with its seal and recorded it as such. That is, the way to the code was correct since the document reached the unit. So it should not be a surprise that there is no signature because on no document of the telegram type is there a signature, as it cannot be coded.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel please wait for the witness to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But these are all instructions and orders which have to do with humanitarian problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking not to start speaking when the witness is still speaking, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Apart from that, if you could find a suitable moment within the next two or three minutes to find a moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I only have one question, and then we can make a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, within the framework of these humanitarian instructions, my question is as follows: Did you ever hear at the corps level, for instance, did you ever hear General Galic insist on the importance to respect the Geneva Conventions specifically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Was it something that happened often, this insistence on the need to observe these conventions and the additional protocols, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fact I'm asking whether how often this was, do you -- is this a leading question, or does this relate to the previous question, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's -- it might be about a person rather than about the frequency, or what's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, it's a leading question, and it follows an earlier leading question, immediately follows. I simply object to leading. That's not an area that is in agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least the question as such suggests -- or the answer might be that's a leading question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Would you please put the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know if General Galic issued --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: One can see from these documents that that was the case, but what is not on paper, what was not written, that happened at the briefings that one had to monitor the situation. I cannot say how frequently that happened, but it was said through the liaison bodies and UNPROFOR, those who had this kind of information, whether every humanitarian convoy has gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will ask this question once again because my question -- because the interpreters did not get my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think you have to ask the question again, but you have to repeat the wordings of your question, since the question has been answered by the witness. So interpretation has reached him, but not in English. So will you please repeat your question. And you, Mr. DP35, you don't have to answer the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My question was -- my question was to know whether the witness was aware of the fact that in the humanitarian area General Galic could perhaps issue other recommendations and instructions. And if so, then which? And I believe we can now take a break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can take a break. Mr. Usher, will you first escort the witness out of the courtroom, and if the parties could just stay for one more second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would just like to make one observation in view of the last reformulation of your question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, in order to clarify the issue of leading questions. I didn't follow you in French, so I do not know whether the English translation is perfectly expressing what you said. But if you're asking a witness whether he was aware of the fact that in the humanitarian area General Galic could perhaps issue other recommendations, if that would be a translation of your question. If it's not, please tell me now so that I don't have to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. My question implied, rather -- I wasn't asking whether he was familiar that the general, but I was asking him if he knew whether General Galic had -- I wasn't asking -- my question was interrogative. It wasn't in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Yes. We'll adjourn until --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'd be grateful for an update as to how much longer the Defence expects to be in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we -- could you inform --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not much. I think a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd say about 15 minutes; not more than that, Mr. President. Ms. Pilipovic is talking in a very low voice and I can't hear her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't follow exactly what the problem -- oh, you couldn't understand Ms. Pilipovic. If you take off your earphone, it will be certainly easier for you to understand what Ms. Pilipovic tells you. I have one final question about the maps to be used, if it would be of any use. If we would use another map, and even if during the break - because that's what I understand you intend to do, Ms. Pilipovic, is to make the witness mark the approximate positions of where the AAD was located - this map cannot be used for that, because it's already in evidence. If there would be another map that could be cruised, it could be -- even be done during the break in the presence of the parties; although, I know that you're alone. But -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm happy to provide the standard Prosecution map that which includes some of the surrounds. And indeed it's something that I would have wanted done before I embarked on extensive cross-examination to have those maps marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we invite the witness to do it during the break. If any of the parties would for that reason miss some coffee or whatever, the Chamber will see whether it will be possible to provide it. But the standard procedure is in the presence of a representative of the Registry or of the staff of the -- one of the legal officers of the Chamber and both -- both parties being present. Before adjourning, I would like to instruct the witness himself on what to do during the break. So if, Mr. Usher, it would be possible -- the curtains are still down. If it would be possible to -- to escort the witness into the courtroom for another second. It takes now two or three minutes, but it will save us certainly more time later on. Ms. Pilipovic, you wanted to ask the witness to indicate on the map with dots and numbers the AAD positions the witness testified about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. He can also indicate them with numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps a dot and a number, because a number might be -- give a rather vague -- especially if the numbers become higher and higher. Number 203 would be easily too vague. It might not be --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can also put an "AAD" indication, "1 AAD," something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we will ask him to make a small cross and put a number next to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, I would like to ask you something; it is the following: You have been asked about the AAD positions. And since we had some difficulties with using the map on the board, I'd like to ask you during the break with a black marker to indicate on another black-and-white map that will be provided to you the positions -- the AAD positions you have told us about. Could you please mark every position with a small cross and put a number next to it, so small cross 1 would be AAD position 1; small cross 2 would be AAD position 2. Could you do that during the break. The parties and someone from the Registry might still be present in the courtroom. Then that saves considerable time when we continue later on. I thank you very much in advance for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have an additional question to you: If you mark these positions on the map, so a cross, then a number, and then a slash, and then add the calibre of the position you just mentioned. So if it would be position number 3, it would be calibre 30 millimetres, would you please indicate that by "3/30." I'll just give an example. Thank you very much in advance for your cooperation. We'll adjourn until five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Awaiting the return of the witness, of which I would like to ask Mr. Usher to escort him into the courtroom. Have the parties had an opportunity to look at the markings made by the witness on the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, while we're waiting for the witness, I would like to take advantage of the time that we have. We would just like to inform the Chamber that with the schedule and given the possibility of contacting the witnesses, the Defence thinks they will conclude with the hearing of witnesses on the 28th of January, or perhaps on the 27th. It depends on how the hearing of the witnesses next week will progress. Then we will have two witnesses outstanding, and we've been allowed to replace them. Our deadline is -- our time limit is three weeks; that is to say, the Prosecution was given three weeks. So I would just like to inform the Trial Chamber that we might have a discussion or a decision on expert witnesses in order to know the schedule for the month of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that mean that all witnesses of fact would be

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have not yet -- the Chamber has not yet responded to the -- to the submissions made by both parties in respect of the -- in respect of the expert witnesses, also because we'd like to do our homework first and see whether there are any additional questions to be put to the parties. But we'll certainly come back to the expert witnesses on very short notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I raised the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Ierace, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that raises an issue that rises immediate clarification. Perhaps in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we perhaps do it during the last five minutes of today's hearing? The witness is now here, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have had a look at the map with the markings on it. The map is now with the -- where is the map? Is it still with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could -- Mr. Usher, could you please give it to the Defence and then also to the Chamber. Yes. If you'd like to show it to General Galic. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber have a look at it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before moving on to the series of questions concerning the map, I would like to go back to where we stopped just before we had the break and I'm going to put the question as follows:

utterances.speaker: THE 28TH OF JANUARY
utterances.text: Witness, if possible, what can you tell us about any dissemination of instructions by the military structure with regard to respecting the Geneva Conventions and other conventions which we are interested in?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's microphone please be put on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please -- well, the witness microphone is on, but perhaps direct it in such a way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say what I've already said in one of my previous answers. We saw documents which had been processed in the command and which had been forwarded to the unit. There were other such documents for sure which we didn't have, which we didn't have access to, and at other meetings they discussed what was given through the record and what was assigned in tasks. These were two ways of forwarding these things: Directly through general documents - this is how the orders would be forwarded - and the second way was at meetings, reports, and they took the form of conclusions, or rather, excerpts from the record. So that's as much I could say about the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE 28TH OF JANUARY
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, with regard to what we call "opening fire," were there any specific instructions which had been given to those who -- at the level of those who used ammunition with regard to the specific issues, that is to say, how to open fire, under which circumstances, et cetera? Do you know anything about this? Are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE 28TH OF JANUARY
utterances.text: What was the nature of these instructions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: In each combat order, in each order, it stated that for AAD units, fire should only be opened if there was an air attack. As I have already said, there were no such attacks during that period, and as far as targets on the ground are concerned, fire should be opened if under threat or if an attack was carried out against our firing positions and against the combat positions in the areas we were located in.

utterances.speaker: THE 28TH OF JANUARY
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would now like to turn to the matter of the positions that you have marked on the map that will be tendered as an exhibit later. I would like you to tell us the positions that you have marked on this map. Are these positions that you were familiar with while you were in the command, that is to say, during the second part of your military career?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes. Each position was directly indicated, and it was possible to make corrections. If I suggested this or with the authorisation of the commander, or on the spot within a position a piece of artillery was under threat, and this was often the case at the sports airport position or the Ilinjaca position. We had to move the weapon 30 to 50 metres because the weapon was under threat. And the points that have been marked on the map are fixed points for the positions which were the basic and central positions. At one point -- at several -- in several places I have marked these positions with a "Y," although you said I should mark these positions with an "X." All the positions marked with an "X" are regiment positions, and I used a "Y" to mark the positions that belonged to the brigade and were in the area of our deployment.

utterances.speaker: THE 28TH OF JANUARY
utterances.text: Thank you, witness, because you have answered the next question I was going to ask you. I wanted to ask you whether there was a difference between the regiment and the brigade, but we can see that you have already mentioned this difference by referring to these two letters. Witness, having examined the map a minute ago, I was able to see that some of the positions that you mentioned were fairly close to what we call the part of the town that was under the control of the BH army. I would like to put to you a more specific question, after having examined this map with you: Weren't there any areas which were nevertheless within range of your batteries? And I mean within the entire area of this part of Sarajevo which was under the control of the enemy force.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: In terms of range, yes. But we measure the range for air targets. If we are examining the ground, the range is interrupted. It's no longer a distant range until you encounter the first obstacle, because my artillery pieces are so sensitive that when they hit an obstacle, the projectile explodes immediately. Any obstacle will diminish the range if there is an obstacle at a distance of 200 metres, then the weapon no longer has a range of 2.000 metres. Therefore, the possible targets, up to a distance of two or three thousand metres, such targets are no longer in my range because in a densely inhabited part of town, in an urban part of the town of Sarajevo the weapons were no longer effective. Artillery that had a certain form of trajectory could be used, but I could only use my pieces of artillery as direct fire, for direct fire.

utterances.speaker: THE 28TH OF JANUARY
utterances.text: And my very last question: If there were targets which were not air targets - and this is purely hypothetical - if you had such targets, what was the nature of these targets? Were they -- were there any such targets that were fixed? What can you tell us about this? Outside of the town too, obviously.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Targets outside of the town. Well, there's a map in front of us with the position Y5. That's Ilidza, as far as I can see. We could fire from these positions in Ilidza only at the part over Butmir, where there was a road which led -- which went above Hrasnica, to Igman. We could fire at part of that road, or we could fire at Butmir Polje, from one artillery piece. We had information, because we were often fired at from there -- we had information according to which they had a weapon called a Zis 70 millimetres, a Zis gun. We knew where it was positioned and we changed the position of our artillery piece, our 40-millimetre piece in order to get this weapon in range, but it was not possible for us because there were obstacles. On the road to Igman, we were only able to target vehicles that had been -- that were of olive-drab colour or camouflage colour for which we could assume that they were transporting ammunition and other explosive devices.

utterances.speaker: THE 28TH OF JANUARY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have another two questions, witness. The first question is as follows: Did you ever shell or fire on the so-called airport area? I'm not referring to the Butmir airport. I'm referring to the Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: THE 28TH OF JANUARY
utterances.text: Thank you. And my second question has to do with the Mojmilo Hill, the so-called Mojmilo Hill. Under whose control was this hill? That's the first part of my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: I think that it was under the control of perhaps two companies. Up to a battalion. It could have been under the control of a battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE 28TH OF JANUARY
utterances.text: Of which army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: THE 28TH OF JANUARY
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you ever able to hit legitimate targets in this Mojmilo area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: THE 28TH OF JANUARY
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: From a position that I have marked with "Y1."

utterances.speaker: THE 28TH OF JANUARY
utterances.text: What's the location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Y1. It's near Lukavica. Here it is, in the lower part of the map, near the barracks. Let me just turn this around. It's this part here. We can see "Y1." That's right. There was a 30-millimetre artillery piece there. Mojmilo was within its -- within their change. We were contacted directly from the building of the commander's. Weapons were either above the command and they were defending the command from weapons from Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: THE 28TH OF JANUARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, Mr. President, I would like to put one last document on the ELMO. I will give it to the usher, if he approaches me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this the last document? Because you indicated what was your last question, then what was your first and your second question, and again you added two more, and now a new document turns up. Is this --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's both. It's the last document and it's the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: THE 28TH OF JANUARY
utterances.text: Witness, I would be grateful if you could tell us, first of all, whether you yourself made this document, and can you comment on all aspects of it. Can you tell us what it represents and in particular why it contains these different symbols and why it contains the UN symbol too.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Well, these are the positions of the Muslim forces on Mojmilo, which was within the area of -- or within the range of the Y1 position. That's a slope which is a little above our barracks, above the Slavica Vajner-Cica barracks. And we were in the barracks in the vicinity about 300 or 400 metres away. We were in the Slobodan Princip-Seljo barracks. And they fired at us from these positions that have been marked with the numbers. You can see that they've been marked as trenches or as orientation points. And in this part, which was under the direct control of our forces, they fired on our command posts and our on road that went through Lukavica. We can see that all these trenches connected by communicating trenches. There were trenches up there, and these orientation points, we have bunkers there. We've got two types that have been marked, orientation points and R. "R" stands for a trench. And a bunker was fortified. It had a loophole which was used to fire at us from Brownings, Browning machine-guns, 12.7-millimetre machine-guns. On the basis of such fire, we determined that there were also machine-guns which had sights, sniper machine-guns, and we established this on the basis of the precision of fire in our area. As far as the marks are concerned, you see the UN feature. Above that position -- there weren't that many houses there. They've been indicated in the horizontal part. But the UN sign indicates that there was a house there where UN members were located. In our area, in our zone, they were French members of the UN. But here to the right, that is to say, the eastern part, there was a house. And later I found out that that part was under the control of the Russians, and for a certain period of time they had even been held in captivity in that part. So the UN sign was there for us, for us to know that they were in the vicinity. But action was taken below them, about 100 metres below them, and fire was opened from these bunkers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please put the microphone on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin indicated that he would have no further questions but did that without putting the microphone on. Mr. Ierace, the issue you had in mind which should be raised immediately, how much time would that take? If it would be more than five minutes, I would suggest that we ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As best as I may expect, it won't be more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please start, if you're ready to cross-examine the witness. Mr. DP35, you'll now be -- we'll at least make a start with being examined by counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: This morning you said that you commenced your responsibilities in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps on the 4th of July, 1992 and up until the 8th of February, 1993 you were the AAD regiment commander. Were you attached to any particular brigade at that stage, in that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: The regiment is immediately attached to the corps command, just like the brigade, it is attached to the corps command. So the regiment, too, is one of the independent units, which is immediately connected to the chief of staff or, rather, to the commander. As the chief, I had links to the chief of staff. And as commander of the regiment, I had links to the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What other differences, if any, were there in terms of your responsibilities between those two positions that you held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Well, the difference mainly consisted in the fact that as a regiment commander I had the batteries and the regiment under my direct command and I was responsible to the corps commander for their use. As the chief of the anti-aircraft defence, this was an organ of the service branch, which was connected to the chief of staff and we would submit proposals concerning the preparation of decisions. And once decisions were taken by the commander, I would then participate in the implementation of these decisions as the organ of command. So the regiment wasn't under my command -- I wasn't commanding the regiment, but I was monitoring how the tasks were being executed, the tasks that the commander had decided on. That was the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was your rank on the 4th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: On the 4th of July I held the rank of major. I was waiting to be promoted to the rank of lieutenant colonel, which I was -- which was conferred on me in autumn.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Which month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: I think the order arrived in September/October, and I held the rank from April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And when you refer to September/October, I take it you mean 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: 1992. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You are recorded on the transcript as saying that you held the rank from April 1992. Should that be from April 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No. April 1992 is when I was promoted to that rank, but the order on promoting me to that rank arrived in autumn 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When your position changed on the 8th of February, 1993, was that a promotion or a demotion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No. In terms of position, it was neither a promotion or a demotion. That's what was necessary then. I was the regiment commander. I had a younger officer who didn't have the appropriate rank, and he was performing the duties of my deputy. During this period, these six or eight months, he became independent to a certain extent and then the commander decided to assign him as acting commander of the regiment and to assign me, designate me as the AAD chief. Those were the needs in the corps. But I often went to control the regiment, to carry out controls in the regiment in order to assist this younger officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You understand that having regard to the description that you gave of each of the job's responsibilities, it might be thought that the responsibility involved with the job that you assumed on the 8th of February, 1993 was somewhat less than the responsibility of the job that you held as the AAD regiment commander. Are you sure there was no demotion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No. It was a higher position, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the -- your replacement as regiment commander was assigned as acting commander. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes. Goran Cosovic, he was a young captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is his name spelled C-o-s-o-v-i-c?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: C with a diacritic mark, yes. Cosovic. You have a C with a diacritic mark at the beginning and a C with a diacritic mark at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How long did he remain in that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Up until the end of the war, up until the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, did you remain in the position that you assumed in February 1993 until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you remain in that position beyond the end of the war? And if so, for how long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35
utterances.text: No, I didn't remain in that position because our corps after the Dayton Agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- For chronological reasons, which we are familiar with. This is after November 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Perhaps we'll hear the response of Mr. Ierace in the absence of the witness. We are close to where we have to have a break anyhow. So I'd first like to ask Mr. Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. Mr. DP35, we'll finish for today, but we'd like to see you back for the continuation of your examination tomorrow morning at 9.00 -- no, tomorrow it's Wednesday, in the afternoon. And Madam Registrar, before making my next mistake, what would be the courtroom? Courtroom II. We'd like to see you back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in another courtroom, but the -- those who are assisting you will tell you where to come, and we'll then continue. Then Mr. Usher, will you please escort the witness as soon as the curtains are finally down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before giving an opportunity to Mr. Ierace to raise the issue he thought he had to raise, perhaps he could first respond to the objection to the last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I withdraw the objection for the sake of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then Mr. Ierace, there was another issue related to the 27/28 January message conveyed to us by the Defence. Could you please express yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I seek firstly to clarify the statement by the Defence is the Defence indicating that the only remaining witnesses after that date indicated will be expert witnesses; in other words, to give an example -- perhaps we could go into closed session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 1.54 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of January, 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 25
